Nuclear Miracles

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We are using nuclear technology to save lives, add a billion rand in exports and make groundbreaking steps forward in several industries in South Africa.

Unique Selling Point:
Nuclear Radioisotope Technology
When you think of nuclear, you might picture dangerous materials, but South Africa is actually at the forefront of using radioisotopes—materials produced during a nuclear reaction—in some truly groundbreaking ways.
Our guide on this scientific journey is Dr Jan Rijn Zeevaart from Necsa. With over 20 years of experience promoting the safe use of this technology, Dr Zeevaart has been involved in numerous groundbreaking projects.
Dr Zeevaart received his PhD in the Netherlands, and since 2002 has been head of the Radiochemistry group at Necsa. He’s co-authored over 100 international publications, has 6 patents and was awarded the South African Chemical Institute’s Raikes Medal (2007) and was part of the international team awarded the Marie Curie award (2018).
He'll lead us through a series of incredible discoveries: from a stage 4 cancer patient being healed, to the eradication of malaria-carrying mosquitoes, and even the use of this technology in ‘save the rhinos’ fight.

We have secured permission to film nuclear reactor at pelindaba.

Summary:
In medicine, we use different elements to create these isotopes—none of which involve uranium.
At this point, the presenter will step in to explain how radioactive isotopes work. “I am here at our nuclear reactor….” They’ll explain that we received special permission to show you exactly where these isotopes are made—at the SAFARI reactor in Pelindaba.
And we’ll meet our main character Dr Zeevaart with a little about his background. And the creation of I-131 radioisotopes which we make here locally. This project earns around 1.3 billion rand per year by selling our locally produced radioisotopes.
And he will show us the lab where the Cyclotron particle accelerator is – this is where the nuclear miracles are born (protons are accelerated in a circular ring to speed close to light, which interacts with material making it radioactive), producing medical radioisotopes.


You had some questions after my pitch I’ve asked Zeevaart to answer:
Jan Zeevaart: Do we produce the isotopes ourselves? Yes, we do. They are made at the SAFARI reactor in Pelindaba, and we’ll get to see the process in action.
Regarding the term “cure” for cancer—there isn’t one single cure. Each type of cancer is unique. However, we can say that we’ve developed groundbreaking treatments for prostate cancer, and the focus is shifting to breast cancer next.
How do cancer cells die? When radioactive material decays, the isotope releases energy, causing breaks in the DNA double strands. This triggers apoptosis, or programmed cell death, which is essentially what kills the cancer cells.
How are the correct cancer cells targeted? The radioactive pharmaceutical or drug is directed by a targeting compound, like a GPS, which guides the isotope to specific areas, allowing it to treat multiple sites as needed.
When it comes to nuclear processes, radioactive decay—fission, or the splitting of an atom—occurs in a nuclear power reactor. In power generation, the focus is on the heat produced during fission, not the byproducts. In contrast, in nuclear medicine, we focus on isolating specific isotopes from that process. For power, uranium is split to generate heat, but in medicine, we extract various isotopes from the same nuclear process and apply them for targeted treatments.


Further information:
We’ll now explore two ways South Africa is using radioactive isotopes to address critical challenges . “The applications/uses are incredibly broad, from anti-poaching to food security... In this story, we’re going to introduce you to just two: medicine… and pest control.” The first is in nuclear medicine, where we’ll introduce the Nuclear Medicine Research Infrastructure (NuMeRI) project. Launched just a few months ago, NuMeRI builds on research collaborations to develop several radiopharmaceuticals for infection imaging and cancer treatment. These have been tested at Steve Biko Academic Hospital under Prof. Mike Sathekge and are now part of the available clinical treatments.
Nuclear isotope tracing to eliminate cancer is a technique used in targeted cancer therapy. This method involves using radioactive isotopes that specifically target cancer cells. The isotope is often attached to a molecule that naturally binds to the cancerous tissue, like a protein or antibody. Once inside the body, the radioactive isotope tracks down the cancer cells, attaching to them and delivering a focused dose of radiation. This process destroys the cancer cells with minimal damage to surrounding healthy tissue.
Again, a radioisotope is a tiny, non-dangerous radioactive molecule. It emits signals as it releases energy (decays), creating a traceable path. This allows us to track and target specific areas, much like using a GPS. Based on this they can target specific cells/processes eradicating the cancer only. We will show this in a SPECT scanner.

We have permission to visit the hospital, where we’ll interview Prof. Sathekge. We’ll also meet a cancer patient who has fully recovered from stage 4 prostate cancer, thanks to this treatment. Each treatment cycle costs about R100,000, and typically requires 3-4 cycles, similar in cost to immunotherapy.
NuMeRI has achieved significant success in prostate cancer trials, with stage 4 patients experiencing full recoveries (we have photos from actual patients). We plan to interview the patient, possibly at their home, depending on their location. We're finalizing the right case study once the media relations person is back from leave this week.
Ending of Act 2 and transition into Act 3:
The presenter will then take us to the next part of the story and we’ll do links at the mosquito rearing facility on how nuclear technology is transforming agriculture. By controlling pests and diseases, enhancing crop production, protecting land and water resources, and ensuring food safety, we are driving innovation in sustainable farming. One key example is the sterile insect technique (SIT), which involves mass rearing, sterilization, and the release of sterile male insects to reduce pest populations. South Africa has already proven this method works, as they combatted fruit flies in the Western Cape previously , but now are using this idea with mosquitos providing an effective, non-GMO solution. But now, the focus is on applying this technique to a new challenge: eradicating malaria .
Necsa is collaborating with the National Institute of Communicable Diseases (NICD) on a groundbreaking project in Jozini, led by Dr Munhenga, aimed at using sterile mosquitos to prevent malaria. Dr Zeevaart explained that unlike nuclear medicine, where we use radiation to kill cells, here we use radiation to sterilize the insects. Sterile males compete with fertile ones, and when they mate, the females don’t produce offspring. According to Dr Munhenga, this approach led to a population crash in the test area compared to the control zone. He’ll share the data with us, giving a clear picture of the results.
We’ll explain these concepts with simple, easy-to-understand graphics, provided by the department. I’d like to work with Mias again, if he’s available, as he’s great at breaking down complex visuals so we can develop new ones.
Dr Munhenga will also join us at the mosquito breeding facility in Modderfontein – we have the access and will be filming the interviews and project there.

Script:


Voice Over/VO: When you hear the word 'nuclear,' what comes to mind?
[explosion]
Maybe it’s the devastating legacy of atomic bombs...

Or the controversy of nuclear power.
[visuals: Fukushima]

But a team of local scientists thinks you should be looking at nuclear differently.

UPSOUND ZEEVAART: 00:16:02 we have cancer patients that are stage 4 that are going home and that is just next to next to a miracle.

UPSOUND SATHEKGE 11:46 Unlike being in the past when nuclear medicine will be holy will have been the last resort it's going to be one of the first resorts

UPSOUND DOUGLAS: 00:05:22 I never thought this day I was standing here, fit
LOURENSA: fit and walking
DOUGLAS: fit and walking
PRESENTER LINK outside building at NECSA: Enter’s frame from the right at the Nuclear Reactor…The applications of using nuclear technology are incredibly broad, from anti poaching to food security and the magic is made right here by South Africans finding solutions to our local problems.
VO: Roughly 10 million people die of cancer every year, making it one of the greatest medical challenges facing humankind.

The most advanced technologies in the world have been brought to bear on fighting cancer - from immunotherapy to gene editing - now, nuclear research is delivering promising results… and South Africa is at the forefront.

PRESENTER LINK: Static one: “The Nuclear Medicine Research Infrastructure or NuMeRI project was launched earlier this year and it's here where the nuclear technology gets put into practice in the treatment of cancer patients

UPSOUND DOUGLAS: Douglas: I was very sick, then they brought me, I was on a wheelchair to this hospital.


VO: In January, Douglas Matyeni, was in the advanced stages of prostate cancer—untreatable by traditional methods.

UPSOUND: Lourensa: Before you started your treatment here where you thought that you were not going to live?
Douglas: I had already given up, because I was 69 kgs my weight, from 110kgs.
01:50 I was as thin as a church mouse (show photo of him)

VO: Prostate cancer progression is measured through a blood test for levels of a marker called PSA. A normal PSA level is below 4, but Douglas’s levels were through the roof—he was knocking on death’s door.

00:01:34,240 Lourensa: how advanced was your cancer?
00:01:37,600 oh well it was very bad because my PSA was about 700
VO: Douglas was selected for a clinical trial open only to patients with prostate cancer that has spread to their bones.
UPSOUND DR SATHEKGE: 00:07:44 Because they have extensive pain metastasis and sometimes near breaking their bones and those patients when they come full time everyday without pain killer they they cannot do anything and they stop working.

VO: Professor Mike Sathekge is the CEO of NuMeRI and a world leading Nuclear Medicine Specialist.

UPSOUND DR SATHEKGE: 00:08:08 After treating them and most of them after one or 2 cycles you see you really see excellent result with the patients relieved with their pain but also with the shrinkage of the lesions
VO: This trial explores a revolutionary approach to imaging and treating cancer.
FADE TO BLACK
UPSOUND SAMMY: 00:03:24 Safari research reactor was actually commissioned 18 March 1965; it will turn 60 years next year.

VO: We are at the South African Nuclear Energy Corporation’s (Necsa) reactor in Pelindaba, North West province called SAFARI-1. Once a site for enriching the uranium for South Africa’s nuclear weapons, now it’s the key to unlocking the lifesaving potential of that technology.

Dr Sammy Malaka manages the SAFARI-1 Research Reactor.
We are one of the best amongst the world that it's available we strive to be available 300 days a year so it's quite a a mean feat

Zeevaart Intv: We doing research and to solve society problems using nuclear technologies.
UPSOUND: ZEEVAART: 01:30 Safari is really the heart of NECSA this is our pride and joy…

VO: Leading the research at Necsa is Radiochemist Professor Jan Rijn Zeevaart. With over 100 international publications to his name, he's a leading figure in the field of nuclear science.

01:30 and that is because we have a neutron factory and we now make a lot of isotopes from that these isotopes are used in industry they used in agriculture

PRESENTER LINK: Behind me is a dashboard providing live updates on how the reactor is operating as you can see all of the indicators are green which tells us that Safari 1 is operating exactly as it should

VO: It all starts with: splitting an atom. Inside this massive tank is the core—about the size of a washing machine—containing uranium rods that fuel the nuclear reaction. But these researchers are looking for something often overlooked: radioactive isotopes, which, simply put, are radioactive atoms that, among other things, can target and destroy cancer cells.

Zeevaart intv: we place the material in their reactor, they become radioactive and now we can do all sorts of things with them.

VO: GRAPHIC: Radioactive isotopes are a byproduct of a nuclear reaction. During that reaction, extra subatomic particles, called neutrons, are released. When another atom is placed inside the reactor, these neutrons fire into it, making it radioactive.
Zeevaarts intv: Lourensa: Is there an element of danger to the research that you're doing?
Zeevaart: In short there's no problem with the safety because we're using a small amount of radioactivity.
VO: South Africa exports these isotopes worldwide, generating significant revenue.
Dr Sammy intv: We occupy just over 20% of isotopes for nuclear medicine. Our customers range from the US, UK, North America that generates a revenue of approximately 1.6 billion to the country.
NTP LINK: The isotopes are brought from the reactor to the processing plant where it's processed and put into this little container from there it goes to a bigger container and it then gets shipped all around the world it needs to reach its final destination within 72 hours
VO: But many of the patients who benefit from these isotopes are much closer to home: less than an hour’s drive away at Steve Biko Academic Hospital.
VISUAL TRANSITION TO STEVE BIKO: AERIALS?
VO: Radioactive isotopes play a role in all the steps needed to combat cancer, including treatment. It starts here, where patients are scanned to locate the cancer.
LINK BY CYCLOTRON: In many cases a person with suspected cancer would be seen to have a pet scanner now that's where the shiny machine comes in it's called a cyclotron and in here radioactive isotopes are produced from there it's put into a glucose solution now the radioactive isotopes bind to the glucose molecules it gets injected into the patient and because cancer loves glucose which is sugar essentially the radioactive isotopes go directly to the cancer cells during the PET scan you're able to get a very detailed image of exactly where the cancer is.
VO: This scan shows the extent of the cancer - which appears as orange - in Douglas’s body before treatment. The isotopes emit energy which the machine uses to trace their location.
UPSOUND: SATHEKGE 00:03:59 so the very same molecule that we use to diagnose will then use it to treat except we change the isotopes.
VO: In other words, a different isotope is now attached to the glucose molecule and injected. The second isotope targets the cancer with sniper-like precision. Radiation breaks down the DNA of the cancer cells, delivering a lethal blow to the tumors. After just two treatments, a new scan shows the cancer is almost gone.
00:02:00,480 what what is your PSa now?
Douglas: the last time I checked it was 6.
Lourensa: so you're a walking miracle?
Douglas: exactly
Lourensa: So is he one of your best patients DOC?
Prof Sathekge: Yes he’s one of the best patients.
00:06:51,400 Douglas is one of our best patients but not only from taking the cancer to being in the mission the quality of health you know the quality of life and the attitude that we have from them.
VO: This method reduces side effects and boosts effectiveness compared to traditional radiation. Each treatment cycle costs about R58 000, with patients typically needing 3 to 4 cycles. Medical aids are already covering these costs

Prof Sathekge intv: so how successful has the study been?
Prof Mike: Very very successful, I mean the overall survival varies from 15 months to people staying for all five years that would have been thought they would be dead in three months or so.

VO: About 1 in 8 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, with many not receiving treatment until it's too late, often relying solely on traditional methods.

INTV Prof Sathekge: Lourensa: it's all about diagnosing cancer and treating cancer at the moment right?
Prof: that is really the crux of it of course we can also do other cardiovascular, neurological, infectious diseases but really the the back of it is really cancer management.
VO: The Dept of Science and Innovation invested R500 million in NuMeRI. With R22 million in annual international funding, this trial is just the start, with the next phase targeting breast cancer.
[small pause]
VO: Once seen as a force of destruction, nuclear technology has evolved into a powerful tool for tackling our greatest medical challenges.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We are using nuclear technology to save lives, add a billion rand in exports and make groundbreaking steps forward in several industries in South Africa.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Nuclear Radioisotope Technology When you think of nuclear, you might picture dangerous materials, but South Africa is actually at the forefront of using radioisotopes—materials produced during a nuclear reaction—in some truly groundbreaking ways. Our guide on this scientific journey is Dr Jan Rijn Zeevaart from Necsa. With over 20 years of experience promoting the safe use of this technology, Dr Zeevaart has been involved in numerous groundbreaking projects. Dr Zeevaart received his PhD in the Netherlands, and since 2002 has been head of the Radiochemistry group at Necsa. He’s co-authored over 100 international publications, has 6 patents and was awarded the South African Chemical Institute’s Raikes Medal (2007) and was part of the international team awarded the Marie Curie award (2018). He'll lead us through a series of incredible discoveries: from a stage 4 cancer patient being healed, to the eradication of malaria-carrying mosquitoes, and even the use of this technology in ‘save the rhinos’ fight. We have secured permission to film nuclear reactor at pelindaba.
metadata.Summary: In medicine, we use different elements to create these isotopes—none of which involve uranium. At this point, the presenter will step in to explain how radioactive isotopes work. “I am here at our nuclear reactor….” They’ll explain that we received special permission to show you exactly where these isotopes are made—at the SAFARI reactor in Pelindaba. And we’ll meet our main character Dr Zeevaart with a little about his background. And the creation of I-131 radioisotopes which we make here locally. This project earns around 1.3 billion rand per year by selling our locally produced radioisotopes. And he will show us the lab where the Cyclotron particle accelerator is – this is where the nuclear miracles are born (protons are accelerated in a circular ring to speed close to light, which interacts with material making it radioactive), producing medical radioisotopes. You had some questions after my pitch I’ve asked Zeevaart to answer: Jan Zeevaart: Do we produce the isotopes ourselves? Yes, we do. They are made at the SAFARI reactor in Pelindaba, and we’ll get to see the process in action. Regarding the term “cure” for cancer—there isn’t one single cure. Each type of cancer is unique. However, we can say that we’ve developed groundbreaking treatments for prostate cancer, and the focus is shifting to breast cancer next. How do cancer cells die? When radioactive material decays, the isotope releases energy, causing breaks in the DNA double strands. This triggers apoptosis, or programmed cell death, which is essentially what kills the cancer cells. How are the correct cancer cells targeted? The radioactive pharmaceutical or drug is directed by a targeting compound, like a GPS, which guides the isotope to specific areas, allowing it to treat multiple sites as needed. When it comes to nuclear processes, radioactive decay—fission, or the splitting of an atom—occurs in a nuclear power reactor. In power generation, the focus is on the heat produced during fission, not the byproducts. In contrast, in nuclear medicine, we focus on isolating specific isotopes from that process. For power, uranium is split to generate heat, but in medicine, we extract various isotopes from the same nuclear process and apply them for targeted treatments.
metadata.Further information: We’ll now explore two ways South Africa is using radioactive isotopes to address critical challenges . “The applications/uses are incredibly broad, from anti-poaching to food security... In this story, we’re going to introduce you to just two: medicine… and pest control.” The first is in nuclear medicine, where we’ll introduce the Nuclear Medicine Research Infrastructure (NuMeRI) project. Launched just a few months ago, NuMeRI builds on research collaborations to develop several radiopharmaceuticals for infection imaging and cancer treatment. These have been tested at Steve Biko Academic Hospital under Prof. Mike Sathekge and are now part of the available clinical treatments. Nuclear isotope tracing to eliminate cancer is a technique used in targeted cancer therapy. This method involves using radioactive isotopes that specifically target cancer cells. The isotope is often attached to a molecule that naturally binds to the cancerous tissue, like a protein or antibody. Once inside the body, the radioactive isotope tracks down the cancer cells, attaching to them and delivering a focused dose of radiation. This process destroys the cancer cells with minimal damage to surrounding healthy tissue. Again, a radioisotope is a tiny, non-dangerous radioactive molecule. It emits signals as it releases energy (decays), creating a traceable path. This allows us to track and target specific areas, much like using a GPS. Based on this they can target specific cells/processes eradicating the cancer only. We will show this in a SPECT scanner. We have permission to visit the hospital, where we’ll interview Prof. Sathekge. We’ll also meet a cancer patient who has fully recovered from stage 4 prostate cancer, thanks to this treatment. Each treatment cycle costs about R100,000, and typically requires 3-4 cycles, similar in cost to immunotherapy. NuMeRI has achieved significant success in prostate cancer trials, with stage 4 patients experiencing full recoveries (we have photos from actual patients). We plan to interview the patient, possibly at their home, depending on their location. We're finalizing the right case study once the media relations person is back from leave this week. Ending of Act 2 and transition into Act 3: The presenter will then take us to the next part of the story and we’ll do links at the mosquito rearing facility on how nuclear technology is transforming agriculture. By controlling pests and diseases, enhancing crop production, protecting land and water resources, and ensuring food safety, we are driving innovation in sustainable farming. One key example is the sterile insect technique (SIT), which involves mass rearing, sterilization, and the release of sterile male insects to reduce pest populations. South Africa has already proven this method works, as they combatted fruit flies in the Western Cape previously , but now are using this idea with mosquitos providing an effective, non-GMO solution. But now, the focus is on applying this technique to a new challenge: eradicating malaria . Necsa is collaborating with the National Institute of Communicable Diseases (NICD) on a groundbreaking project in Jozini, led by Dr Munhenga, aimed at using sterile mosquitos to prevent malaria. Dr Zeevaart explained that unlike nuclear medicine, where we use radiation to kill cells, here we use radiation to sterilize the insects. Sterile males compete with fertile ones, and when they mate, the females don’t produce offspring. According to Dr Munhenga, this approach led to a population crash in the test area compared to the control zone. He’ll share the data with us, giving a clear picture of the results. We’ll explain these concepts with simple, easy-to-understand graphics, provided by the department. I’d like to work with Mias again, if he’s available, as he’s great at breaking down complex visuals so we can develop new ones. Dr Munhenga will also join us at the mosquito breeding facility in Modderfontein – we have the access and will be filming the interviews and project there.
